title: Trump allows Hegseth aide to bypass law
description_short: Trump allows Hegseth aide to bypass law
description_medium: A Washington Post report says Donald Trump authorized a waiver allowing Marine Corps Col. Ricky D. Buria to retire in July 2025 with the rank of colonel, which he had held since November 2024. Federal law generally requires three years in grade, with exceptions for extreme hardship or unusual circumstances. The report does not identify the waiver’s stated basis.
description_long: Marine Corps Col. Ricky D. Buria’s retirement became official in July 2025 after President Donald Trump authorized a waiver of the usual three-year service requirement for retiring at his current rank, according to The Washington Post. Buria had held the rank of colonel since November 2024. The law allows a presidential waiver in cases involving “extreme hardship or exceptional or unusual circumstances,” but the report did not identify a specific finding that Buria met either condition. Buria had served as a top aide to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and submitted retirement paperwork in April while seeking to become Hegseth’s chief of staff. The White House instead blocked him from that permanent position, though he held the role in an acting capacity. The waiver does not increase his pension, which is calculated using his pay over the final three years of military service, but it permits him to retain the colonel title.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump allows Hegseth aide to bypass law

notes: needs_context: an archived Washington Post report states Buria’s retirement became official in July 2025 and that Trump authorized a waiver under the statutory hardship or unusual-circumstances exception. The official waiver document and its specific rationale are not supplied.

title: Trump Army shuts down entire social media accounts because of one post featuring Democrat war hero Sen. Tammy Duckworth
description_short: Trump Army shuts down entire social media accounts because of one post featuring Democrat war hero Sen. Tammy Duckworth
description_medium: The Hill reported that Army Secretary Dan Driscoll ordered all Soldier for Life social media accounts taken offline after criticism of a post honoring Sen. Tammy Duckworth. The Army said it was removing accounts without qualified public-affairs staff under a December 2025 directive; a Defense Department source separately told The Hill that the backlash to the Duckworth post prompted Driscoll’s action. The accounts’ later status is not reported.
description_long: After Soldier for Life shared a post honoring Sen. Tammy Duckworth, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll ordered the unit’s social media accounts taken offline, The Hill reported on April 15, 2026. The post described Duckworth’s life and military service; critics objected to the Army’s tribute to the Illinois Democrat and Iraq War veteran. A Defense Department source familiar with the decision told The Hill that Driscoll acted after the negative reaction. The Army gave another explanation: it said the account was not directly managed by qualified personnel and had been removed as part of a broader review. The Hill reported that an Army directive signed in December 2025 required accounts without an assigned public-affairs professional to deactivate and archive by February 28, 2026. The differing accounts leave unclear whether the Duckworth post determined this specific shutdown or whether the accounts were being closed under a department-wide policy.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Army shuts down entire social media accounts because of one post featuring Democrat war hero Sen. Tammy Duckworth
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Army shuts down entire social media accounts because of one post featuring Democrat war hero Sen. Tammy Duckworth

notes: needs_context: the archived Hill report records two explanations: the Army cited a December 2025 account-management directive, while a Defense Department source said Driscoll acted after backlash to the Duckworth post. It confirms the accounts were taken offline but gives no later restoration decision or duration.

title: A Chaotic Cabinet: Four Major Departures in Six Months
description_short: A Chaotic Cabinet: Four Major Departures in Six Months
description_medium: By late June 2026, the instability of Trump's second-term Cabinet became glaringly obvious. Within just the first half of the year, four top officials had either been fired or resigned under pressure: Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem (fired), Attorney General Pam Bondi (removed), Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer (resigned amidst an IG probe), and DNI Tulsi Gabbard (resigned over Iran). This unprecedented turnover left critical departments rudderless and run by unconfirmed acting secretaries like Todd Blanche at the DOJ, allowing Trump to bypass Senate confirmation and consolidate executive power.

title: DOJ Released 1,000+ Trump Mentions from Suppressed Epstein Files
description_short: DOJ Released 1,000+ Trump Mentions from Suppressed Epstein Files
description_medium: A February 2026 PBS NewsHour segment summarized an NPR investigation alleging that the Justice Department withheld Epstein files containing allegations involving Donald Trump. The transcript describes a heavily redacted FBI interview tied to a woman’s allegation of abuse as a minor; the White House denied the allegation. The record numbers were compared with material previously provided to Ghislaine Maxwell’s lawyers.
description_long: In February 2026, NPR reported that the Justice Department had not released some Epstein-related records containing allegations involving President Donald Trump. A PBS NewsHour interview with Miami Herald reporter Julie K. Brown described an FBI interview with a woman who said she had been assaulted by Trump when she was 13. Brown said one interview appeared in released files but was heavily redacted, making it difficult to determine what the witness told the FBI. She also described how an independent journalist compared identifying numbers on the records with documents prosecutors had previously produced to Ghislaine Maxwell’s defense team. Democrats on the House Oversight Committee said the withholding could be unlawful; the White House denied the underlying allegation. Brown said extensive redactions prevent the public from seeing the full picture of what investigators learned and how Epstein’s network operated.

title: Trump Pardons Corrupt New Jersey Politicians
description_short: Trump Pardons Corrupt New Jersey Politicians
description_medium: In early 2025, Trump issued pardons for several New Jersey politicians convicted of corruption charges, including figures connected to the Essex County Democratic machine. The pardons were widely interpreted as political transactions with Democratic officials who had remained cooperative with Trump's agenda. Legal ethics experts noted the pardons appeared to reward political loyalty rather than address miscarriages of justice. The episode added to a broader pattern of Trump using the pardon power transactionally. The pardoned individuals had been convicted of bribery and fraud related to government contracts.
